slides.title: Your project after Day 1
body: Bronze preserves 144 trip receipts for 72 trip IDs.
Drivers and location events have their own grains.
Today you create trusted Silver and dbt evidence.
slides.notes: Restore your own Day 1 handoff if Colab has started a new runtime. Confirm that the pointer and the actual Delta folders both exist. The project continues from the same source release. Typing fields is the first transformation; it does not itself remove duplicate receipts.

slides.title: Day 2 outcomes
body: Design the Bronze-to-Silver ELT path.
Handle keys, relationships, replays and late arrivals.
Run and explain dbt models and tests.
slides.notes: LO3 is the main objective, with Delta practice supporting LO4 and the cumulative build supporting LO8. By the end, your trusted table should contain 75 trips and 1,875.60 SAR. You will prove the replay behavior and retain separate dbt evidence rather than assuming that a Python transformation proves dbt ran.

slides.title: ETL and ELT
body: Extract obtains the source data.
Load preserves it in a destination.
Transform applies structure and business meaning.
slides.notes: Masar uses ELT by keeping raw records in Bronze before applying Spark transformations. ETL can still be appropriate when the destination must never receive a prohibited field or needs a transformed input. The order follows the requirements. ELT does not mean that every available field should be collected or retained forever.

slides.title: The Silver contract
body: One row represents one trip_id.
Fares use decimal values and durations use seconds.
Every trip must have a valid driver relationship.
slides.notes: Read DATA_CONTRACT.md before changing code. A schema gives a field a type, while the contract also defines its meaning, unit and valid relationship. Zero fares are allowed by this fixture; negative fares are not. Distances and durations must be positive. A missing driver key requires investigation before enrichment.

slides.title: Staging translates the fields
body: Parse timestamps and retain their intended timezone meaning.
Normalize known city labels.
Check casts and required values before choosing a record.
slides.notes: The source contains known label variants such as surrounding spaces and lower-case letters. Normalize them in staging while retaining raw Bronze. A failed cast can become a missing value, so test the result. Canonical timestamps use UTC while business dates follow the trip start in Asia/Riyadh.

slides.title: Joins can change the result
body: A duplicate driver key can multiply trip rows.
A missing driver can remove or leave an unmatched trip.
Check keys and relationships before using the join.
slides.notes: Do not assume that a join preserves the left-hand count. First establish uniqueness in the driver table and identify missing relationships. A valid many-to-one trip-to-driver join preserves the trip-grain population. Use count and key checks before and after enrichment, then inspect representative business values.

slides.title: Duplicates and conflicts
body: Identical receipts can map to one business record.
A later revision can represent an approved change.
Equal revisions with different values need investigation.
slides.notes: Blindly dropping duplicates by trip_id can select the wrong fare. The current Day 2 inputs have identical replayed values; Day 3 introduces correction precedence. Explain the chosen ordering and check for conflicts before merging. A deterministic choice is valuable only when its business rule is correct.

slides.title: Late arrival and event date
body: Occurrence time describes when a trip happened.
Arrival time describes when the pipeline received it.
Reports and incremental filters can need different clocks.
slides.notes: Three June 1 trips arrive in the fixed scenario on June 4. The trip-date report should assign them to June 1. An incremental arrival filter must still include them. Filtering only trips whose business date equals today would miss historical late data and may return nothing for this fixed dataset.

slides.title: Quick activity: make the decision
body: Choose the trip business key: driver_id, trip date or trip_id. Explain one collision the wrong key would create.
Think: 1 minute. Compare: 2 minutes. Discuss: 2 minutes.
slides.notes: Use the project terms rather than naming tools without a reason. State your choice and the assumption behind it. The activity is part of the explanation time and has no separate project mark.

slides.title: Activity answer
body: Use trip_id. A driver can complete many trips and a date can contain many trips, so neither uniquely identifies a trip.
slides.notes: Compare the reasoning as well as the final choice. If you selected another answer, identify which meaning of a row, time boundary or business rule led to it. The project will provide an observable example of this decision.

slides.title: Idempotent business processing
body: Rerunning the same logical input preserves the result.
New delivery receipts can exist without new trips.
Compare business content, not only a row count.
slides.notes: The Silver exercise checks the base, transform rerun, late batch, same-batch retry and new late redelivery. Counts alone can hide changed fares or swapped city assignments. Inspect the checked business fields and the totals together. A new delivery can grow Bronze while Silver stays at the same 75 keys.

slides.title: The five Silver scenarios
body: Base and transform rerun: 72 trips, SAR 1,794.60.
Late batch: 75 trips, SAR 1,875.60.
Retries and redelivery: still 75 trips.
slides.notes: The receipt counts progress 144, 144, 147, 147, 150. The same committed batch retry does not add receipts; a new delivery ID records another arrival. Both routes must preserve the 75 business trips after the late batch. Record what changed at each layer and why those changes differ.

slides.title: dbt models and dependencies
body: A model expresses a transformation.
source() refers to a declared existing source.
ref() connects one model to another.
slides.notes: The actual dbt exercise uses six models and three source tables. source() does not ingest a CSV by itself; the runner prepares the relations first. ref() allows dbt to establish dependencies and resolve relation names. Follow one field from staging through the Silver model into the city-day mart.

slides.title: dbt tests and freshness
body: Test keys, missing values and relationships.
Reconcile marts with their input population.
Measure freshness using a named arrival clock.
slides.notes: The supplied project contains generic tests and seven SQL tests. Source freshness is a separate operation from a build. The exercise uses ingestion time and a fixed scenario clock, with documented warning and error thresholds. A test checks a stated condition; a pass does not prove that every possible business rule was examined.

slides.title: Incremental lookback
body: The course uses a three-day ingestion lookback.
The business key still controls the MERGE result.
Older corrections can require deliberate reprocessing.
slides.notes: An incremental filter reduces the scanned source, while the key and merge behavior control duplicate effects. These are different responsibilities. A bounded lookback can miss a change arriving outside its policy window. The supplied optional all-history reprocessing path makes that limitation explicit rather than hiding it.

slides.title: Separate the two implementations
body: PySpark creates the continuing Silver table.
dbt demonstrates the same principles in an isolated workspace.
Retain real dbt results for assessment.
slides.notes: The dbt runner uses copies of the original Bronze snapshots and does not replace the corrected main project state. It runs within its documented Spark-session context. Starting an unrelated dbt process can lose the in-memory source catalog. Inspect the actual base/rerun/late/late_replay reports and preserve the generated documentation.

slides.title: Your end-of-lab question
body: Silver has 75 trips after three late trips arrive. Will replaying that same late data increase the result to 78?
Record your first answer and observed evidence in student/day02/REFLECTION.md.
slides.notes: Work from your own run before reading the next slide. State the relevant grain, identity or time boundary. A count, fare, validation field or short query result can support your explanation. This reflection contributes one point to the 100-point project.

slides.title: Model answer
body: No. Silver stays at 75 because the replay carries the same trip IDs and identical business values. Receipt counts may increase for a new delivery; the business count must not.
slides.notes: Keep your initial answer and add a correction if needed. Explain the difference using a specific observed result from your notebook or report. The model answer is a learning reference, not a substitute for execution evidence.
